item.title: Syncing Files from macOS to Fedora Linux with rsync and SSH
item.description:
When transferring files between a macOS workstation (such as my MacBook Air ankaa) and a Fedora Linux machine (my Lenovo ThinkPad T450 taylor), rsync over SSH provides fast, incremental synchronization. Once the taylor host alias is configured in ~/.ssh/config, rsync automatically inherits your target IP address (192.168.0.10), username, and custom identity key without requiring explicit connection flags on every run.

The Recommended Command Structure (Short Flags)

The standard pattern for copying files from macOS to a remote Linux host uses compact short options:

rsync -avzP /path/to/local/source/ taylor:/path/to/remote/destination/

Flag Breakdown (-avzP)

  • `-a` (archive mode): Preserves file permissions, ownership, timestamps, and symbolic links recursively.
  • `-v` (verbose): Displays which files are being transferred.
  • `-z` (compress): Compresses data in transit to speed up transfers over Wi-Fi or LAN.
  • `-P` (progress and partial): Displays real-time progress bars and retains partially transferred files to allow resuming interrupted transfers.

Common Use Cases and Trailing Slashes

  1. Transferring a Single File:

    rsync -avzP ~/Downloads/document.pdf taylor:~/Downloads/

  2. Transferring an Entire Folder:

    Pay close attention to the trailing slash (/) on the source directory:

    • Copy the contents of a directory into a target folder (note the trailing slash on Photos/):

      rsync -avzP ~/Photos/ taylor:~/Pictures/

      (Result: Files inside ``~/Photos/`` are placed directly inside ``~/Pictures/`` on ``taylor``).

    • Copy the directory itself as a subdirectory (no trailing slash on Photos):

      rsync -avzP ~/Photos taylor:~/Pictures/

      (Result: Creates ``~/Pictures/Photos/`` on ``taylor``).

Safe Verification: Run a Dry Run First (-n)

To preview which files will be copied or updated without modifying anything on disk, pass the -n (or --dry-run) flag:

rsync -avzPn ~/Documents/ taylor:~/Documents/

Once you confirm the file list looks accurate, remove the n flag to perform the live transfer.

Short Flags vs. Long Options

Short options (like -a, -v, -z) are single-letter abbreviations designed for quick terminal input. Long options (like --archive, --verbose, --compress) perform the exact same operations while remaining self-documenting and easier to read in scripts and documentation.

Short Flag Equivalent Long Option What It Does
-a --archive Enables recursion and preserves permissions, modification times, ownership, and symlinks.
-v --verbose Displays detailed information about which files are being transferred.
-z --compress Compresses file data during network transit to speed up transfer times over Wi-Fi.
-P --progress --partial Combined shortcut: --progress shows the live bar; --partial keeps incomplete files if the connection breaks for resuming.
-n --dry-run Performs a trial run showing what would change without transferring or modifying any files.
-u --update Skips files that are already newer on the destination host (taylor).

What --update Adds to Your Workflow

Adding --update instructs rsync to compare file timestamps across both machines:

  • If a file on taylor is newer than the corresponding file on your Mac, rsync will not overwrite it.
  • This prevents accidentally rolling back recent edits made directly on the remote Linux workstation.

Recommended Command Structure (Long Options)

Using explicit long options, the standard transfer syntax becomes:

rsync --archive --verbose --update --compress --progress --partial /path/to/local/source/ taylor:/path/to/remote/destination/

Note

--compress is optional over fast local networks, though still recommended when transferring large text files, source code repositories, or scripts.

Long-Option Use Cases and Dry Runs

  1. Transferring a Single File:

    rsync --archive --verbose --update --progress --partial ~/Downloads/document.pdf taylor:~/Downloads/

  2. Transferring Directory Contents vs. Subdirectories:

    • Copy contents directly (trailing slash on Photos/):

      rsync --archive --verbose --update --compress --progress --partial ~/Photos/ taylor:~/Pictures/

    • Copy the directory itself (no trailing slash on Photos):

      rsync --archive --verbose --update --compress --progress --partial ~/Photos taylor:~/Pictures/

  3. Running a Dry Run with Long Options:

    rsync --dry-run --archive --verbose --update --progress --partial ~/Documents/ taylor:~/Documents/

Filtering macOS Metadata Files

macOS automatically generates hidden metadata files such as .DS_Store and .localized that clutter Linux directories. You can exclude them per command or configure a permanent global exclusion list.

Option 1: Inline Exclusions (Per-Command)

Pass individual --exclude parameters directly to rsync:

rsync --archive --verbose --update --progress --partial \
  --exclude='.DS_Store' \
  --exclude='.localized' \
  --exclude='._*' \
  --exclude='.CFUserTextEncoding' \
  ~/Desktop/ taylor:~/Desktop/

Common macOS metadata files to exclude include:

  • .DS_Store (Finder folder display settings)
  • .localized (system folder localization hints)
  • ._* (AppleDouble resource fork files created on non-HFS/APFS volumes)
  • .CFUserTextEncoding (user text encoding preferences)
  • .Trashes and .Spotlight-V100 (system trash and Spotlight index directories)

One-Liner with Zsh Brace Expansion

Because macOS uses zsh as its default shell, you can collapse multiple --exclude flags into a single brace expansion one-liner:

rsync --archive --verbose --update --progress --partial --exclude={'.DS_Store','.localized','._*','.CFUserTextEncoding'} ~/Desktop/ taylor:~/Desktop/

The shell expands {...} into separate --exclude arguments before executing rsync.

Option 2: Permanent Global Exclusion List (Recommended)

To avoid typing exclusion flags repeatedly, define a global ignore file in your home directory and alias rsync in ~/.zshrc.

  1. Create ``~/.rsync-exclude`` on macOS:

    cat << 'EOF' > ~/.rsync-exclude
.DS_Store
.localized
._*
.CFUserTextEncoding
.Trashes
.Spotlight-V100
EOF

  2. Add an alias to ``~/.zshrc``:

    Open ~/.zshrc in your editor:

    nano ~/.zshrc

    Append the following line and save the file:

    alias rsync='rsync --exclude-from="$HOME/.rsync-exclude"'

    Reload your shell configuration:

    source ~/.zshrc

  3. Run your standard sync command:

    rsync --archive --verbose --update --progress --partial ~/Desktop/ taylor:~/Desktop/

Cleaning Up Existing Metadata Files on Linux

If macOS metadata files were already synced to taylor previously, you can remove them remotely via SSH:

ssh taylor "find ~/Desktop -name '.DS_Store' -o -name '.localized' -delete"

SSH Host Key Troubleshooting and Connection Verification

When reinstalling Fedora Linux on taylor while retaining the same local IP address (192.168.0.10), SSH generates a new host key fingerprint. Attempting to copy keys or connect from ankaa will trigger a remote host identification warning because the stored fingerprint in ~/.ssh/known_hosts no longer matches.

Step 1: Remove the Stale Host Key Entry

Clear the old fingerprint for 192.168.0.10 from ankaa:

ssh-keygen -R 192.168.0.10

This removes the outdated entry from ~/.ssh/known_hosts and saves a backup copy of the previous file.

Step 2: Copy Your Public Key and Accept the New Fingerprint

Re-run ssh-copy-id using your custom-named public key:

ssh-copy-id -i ~/.ssh/porfirio@ankaa.pub porfirio@192.168.0.10

Type yes when prompted to trust the new host fingerprint, then enter your Fedora password to install the public key on taylor.

Step 3: Configure ~/.ssh/config and Test Connections

Ensure your SSH client configuration on ankaa points to the private key file (without the .pub extension):

nano ~/.ssh/config

Host taylor
    HostName 192.168.0.10
    User porfirio
    IdentityFile ~/.ssh/porfirio@ankaa

Enforce strict permissions on the configuration file:

chmod 600 ~/.ssh/config

You can now verify passwordless authentication using three methods:

  1. Direct connection with explicit identity flag:

    ssh -i ~/.ssh/porfirio@ankaa porfirio@192.168.0.10

  2. Non-interactive remote command execution:

    ssh -i ~/.ssh/porfirio@ankaa porfirio@192.168.0.10 "hostname; uptime"

  3. Alias-based connection:

    ssh taylor

If SSH still prompts for a password, run the connection in verbose mode (-v) to inspect key negotiation:

ssh -v -i ~/.ssh/porfirio@ankaa porfirio@192.168.0.10

item.title: Seamless SSH Agent Forwarding and Keychain Management Between macOS and Linux
item.description:
When connecting via SSH from a primary workstation to a remote Linux machine, the remote shell initializes as an isolated environment. By default, it does not inherit your local machine's active ssh-agent session, nor does it automatically spawn a new agent or load custom-named private keys unless explicitly configured to do so.

For example, when I SSH from my MacBook Air (ankaa) into my Lenovo ThinkPad T450 running Fedora Linux (taylor) to work on my Pelican blog repository, running git fetch or git push against GitHub on taylor will fail with Permission denied (publickey) if no active agent socket is available. While running eval "$(ssh-agent -s)" and ssh-add manually on the remote host solves the issue for a single session, OpenSSH provides a much cleaner, permanent workflow via client configuration.

By combining agent forwarding on the client side with native OS credential integration, you can authenticate Git operations and secondary SSH jumps from a remote Linux host without ever copying private keys onto it.

Core SSH Client Directives

To manage SSH key lifecycles automatically on macOS and forward credentials securely to a Linux host, three primary directives in ~/.ssh/config work together:

1. AddKeysToAgent yes

  • What it does: Automatically loads your private SSH key into the running ssh-agent memory the first time you use it.
  • Why it matters: Instead of manually running ssh-add after every system reboot or new terminal session, OpenSSH silently registers the key the moment you initiate a connection.

2. UseKeychain yes

  • What it does: Integrates OpenSSH with native macOS Keychain Services.
  • Why it matters: When you unlock an encrypted SSH key with its passphrase on macOS, the passphrase is stored securely in your Keychain. On subsequent logins or reboots, ssh-agent retrieves the passphrase automatically so you do not have to re-enter it.

Note

UseKeychain is a macOS-specific OpenSSH option. If you share your ~/.ssh/config across Linux systems like taylor, OpenSSH on Linux will ignore it or require IgnoreUnknown UseKeychain at the top of the configuration file.

3. ForwardAgent yes

  • What it does: Passes your local machine's active ssh-agent socket through the encrypted SSH tunnel to the remote host.
  • Why it matters: Remote processes—such as git interacting with GitHub—can request cryptographic signatures directly from your local agent. Your private key never leaves your local machine; only authentication challenges and signatures traverse the encrypted channel.

Warning

Only enable ForwardAgent yes on trusted remote hosts where you control root access, as a privileged user on the remote machine could temporarily access the forwarded socket while your session is active.

Configuring the Client Machine (macOS)

To put this workflow into practice, configure your SSH client on the initiating machine. Using my setup as a working example, I configure ~/.ssh/config on ankaa (macOS) to define connection parameters for taylor (Fedora Linux).

Step 1: Edit ~/.ssh/config

Open your SSH client configuration file on your local machine:

nano ~/.ssh/config

Add a host definition block specifying the target address, user, identity file, and agent directives:

Host taylor
    HostName <taylor-ip-or-hostname>
    User porfirio
    IdentityFile ~/.ssh/id_ed25519
    AddKeysToAgent yes
    UseKeychain yes
    ForwardAgent yes

(Replace ``<taylor-ip-or-hostname>`` and ``porfirio`` with your target host's IP address or local hostname and username).

Step 2: Enforce Strict Configuration Permissions

OpenSSH enforces StrictModes on configuration files as well as keys. Ensure your ~/.ssh/config file is readable and writable only by your user account:

chmod 600 ~/.ssh/config

Verifying the Workflow on the Remote Host

Once the configuration block is saved on ankaa, connecting and authenticating remote Git operations requires zero manual agent management:

  1. Initiate the SSH connection from ankaa:

    ssh taylor

  2. macOS automatically loads ~/.ssh/id_ed25519 into ssh-agent, unlocks it via Keychain, and forwards the agent socket to taylor.

  3. On taylor, verify that the forwarded identity is visible to the remote shell:

    ssh-add -l

  4. Navigate to a repository and run remote Git operations directly against GitHub without storing local keys on taylor:

    cd ~/gitRepos/github.com/porfiriopaiz/site
git fetch origin
git switch devel

Finishing Touches

With AddKeysToAgent, UseKeychain, and ForwardAgent properly configured, your primary workstation acts as a single, secure credential vault. You can seamlessly administer remote Linux systems and interact with authenticated Git repositories while keeping your private keys isolated on a single physical device.

item.title: Backing Up and Restoring SSH Keys
item.description:
When setting up a fresh system like my Lenovo ThinkPad T450 (named taylor) running Fedora Linux 44 (Workstation Edition), transferring cryptographic identities safely is a top priority. When hardening SSH, the strictness of file permissions is enforced directly by OpenSSH's StrictModes check. If permissions are too open, SSH will reject key usage with errors like permissions being too open.

OpenSSH Permission Requirements

Here are the minimal and recommended permissions required for secure SSH key directory and file operations on your system.

The SSH Directory (~/.ssh)

  • Minimal/Recommended Permission: 700 (drwx------).
  • Access Level: Only the file owner can read, write, and execute the directory, leaving group and others with zero access.
  • Ownership: Must be owned by the active user account utilizing the keys.
chmod 700 ~/.ssh
chown -R $USER:$USER ~/.ssh

Files Within the SSH Directory

Permissions vary depending on whether the file contains private data, public data, or configuration settings:

  • Private Keys (id_ed25519, id_rsa): Mode 600 (or 400) for owner read/write or read-only access, barring all others.
  • Public Keys (id_ed25519.pub, id_rsa.pub): Mode 644 allowing owner read/write and group/others read-only access.
  • Authorized Keys (authorized_keys): Mode 600 for owner read/write only.
  • Config / Known Hosts (config, known_hosts): Mode 600.

Note

For private key files, the absolute minimum required permission for standard SSH operations is 400 (-r--------). However, 600 is standard because it allows updating configurations without modifying permission bits first.

Parent Directory Constraints

OpenSSH also validates the permissions of parent directories in the path leading up to ~/.ssh. Your home directory must not be writable by group or world, with a maximum allowable mode of 755 or 750. If the home directory has overly open permissions, SSH will refuse key authentication even if ~/.ssh is set to 700.

chmod 750 /home/$USER

Backing Up and Restoring via External USB

To transfer your .ssh directory to an external USB drive from Fedora 44 and later restore it to taylor, standard copying tools can cause ownership mismatches or strip permission bits. Using rsync with the -p (--perms) flag ensures permission bits transfer intact while writing files directly under your current logged-in user.

Using rsync for Backup and Restoration

Assuming your USB directory mount path points to your target location, run the copy operation while preserving permissions:

rsync -rp /path/to/source/.ssh/ /path/to/destination/.ssh/

The flag breakdown includes:

  • `-r` (`--recursive`): Recurses into subdirectories and copies all files.
  • `-p` (`--perms`): Preserves explicit file permission modes.
  • No `-o`/`-g`: Running as a normal user without sudo automatically assigns your current $USER and primary group as the owner.

Alternative Using cp

If rsync is not available, you can perform the copy with cp:

cp -r --preserve=mode /path/to/source/.ssh /path/to/destination/.ssh

Post-Restore Verification and Hardening

After restoring your keys to taylor from the USB drive, perform a post-copy safety check and apply mass hardening commands to satisfy OpenSSH strict mode checks.

Inspection and Hardening Commands

Verify file permissions and apply the mass hardening script:

# 1. Inspect restored files
ls -la ~/.ssh

# 2. Set directory to 700 and private keys to 600
chmod 700 ~/.ssh
chmod 600 ~/.ssh/id_* 2>/dev/null || true
chmod 644 ~/.ssh/*.pub 2>/dev/null || true

# 3. Ensure proper user ownership
chown -R $USER:$USER ~/.ssh

Establishing Remote SSH Key Authentication

To connect from another machine—such as your MacBook Pro (running macOS)—to your Lenovo ThinkPad taylor (running Fedora 44) using SSH keys, you need to configure network access, verify the SSH daemon, and copy your public key.

Step 1: Find the IP Addresses

First, identify the local IP addresses of both systems.

On your Lenovo ThinkPad (Fedora Linux), open a terminal and run:

hostname -I

(Alternatively, use ``ip a`` and look for the ``inet`` address under your Wi-Fi or Ethernet interface).

On your MacBook Pro (macOS), open Terminal and run:

ipconfig getifaddr en0

(If connected via Wi-Fi, ``en0`` is typically your Wi-Fi interface).

Step 2: Ensure SSH Server is Running on Fedora

Before copying your key, ensure your ThinkPad allows incoming SSH connections. On your ThinkPad, run:

# Check if SSH daemon is active
systemctl status sshd

# If it is not active, start and enable it:
sudo systemctl enable --now sshd

# Ensure Fedora's firewall allows SSH traffic:
sudo firewall-cmd --add-service=ssh --permanent
sudo firewall-cmd --reload

Step 3: Copy Your Key from MacBook Pro to ThinkPad

Because your key file may have a custom name (such as porfirio@altair.pub instead of the default id_ed25519.pub), you must pass the -i flag to specify it.

Run this command from your MacBook Pro Terminal (replace username with your Fedora username and 192.168.1.50 with your ThinkPad's IP):

ssh-copy-id -i ~/.ssh/porfirio@altair.pub username@192.168.1.50
  1. Confirm the connection prompt by typing yes and hitting Enter.
  2. Enter your Fedora user password when prompted.
  3. The key will be installed into ~/.ssh/authorized_keys on your ThinkPad.

Step 4: Configure ~/.ssh/config on Your MacBook Pro

Since your key file has a custom name, macOS will not automatically use it when running a standard SSH connection. To make connecting seamless, add an entry to your ~/.ssh/config file on your MacBook Pro:

  1. Open the configuration file on your Mac:

    nano ~/.ssh/config

  2. Add the following host block:

    Host taylor
    HostName 192.168.1.50
    User username
    IdentityFile ~/.ssh/porfirio@altair

    (Replace ``192.168.1.50`` with your ThinkPad's IP and ``username`` with your Fedora account name).

  3. Save and exit (Ctrl + O, Enter, then Ctrl + X).

Step 5: Test Passwordless SSH

Now, from your MacBook Pro, you can connect passwordlessly by running:

ssh taylor

Finishing Touches

With these steps completed on Fedora 44, your SSH keys are safely backed up, restored, and fully optimized for secure remote connections.
